title: Batch uniformization latency tail synthesis labbook
content:
Purpose / elevator
This is an experiment log exploring a lightweight 'batch uniformization' approach: bias the scheduler to smooth batch-size variance across time-slices to see if we can lower p99 and p999 tail latency without paying too much cost in throughput or fairness.

High-level hypothesis
- Variance in instantaneous batch sizes (microbursts of large batches followed by long runs of small batches) amplifies tail latency because large batches delay KV cache priming for subsequent sequences and increase scheduling jitter.
- If we force the scheduler to more uniformly produce medium-sized batches (trade small short batches for slightly larger ones and cap very large batches), the long tail should shrink.
- We may hurt average latency (p50/p95) for some classes; fairness policy must ensure no long starvation.

What 'uniformization' means here
- Soft cap: a tunable soft cap on per-slot batch size (cap_s), above which new arrivals are placed preferentially into adjacent slot or delayed by a tiny jitter.
- Age-bias: requests accrue an "age" weight; after age_threshold (ms) a request gets priority to ensure not starved.
- Timeout annealing: initial per-slot timeout t0 that reduces by factor alpha after each accepted batch in a short epoch to avoid always waiting max_timeout.

Experiment matrix (primary sweeps)
- cap_s: [8, 16, 32, none]
- base_timeout_ms: [3, 6, 12]
- age_threshold_ms: [20, 50, 100]
- fairness_mode: [none, age-priority, token-fairshare]
- annealing_alpha: [1.0 (no anneal), 0.75, 0.5]
- traffic shapes: steady low qps (50 rps), steady medium qps (250 rps), spikey (bursts to 1500 rps every 10s), realistic production trace (sampled week).

Metrics collected
- Per-slot: batch_size distribution, batch_wait_time (ms), per-request age at dispatch
- End-to-end: p50/p90/p95/p99/p999 latency for first-byte (start-of-token) and tail (completion)
- Cost: GPU utilization (%) and tokens/sec per-GPU
- Fairness: fraction of requests delayed > age_threshold_ms, number of timeouts triggered per request
- Microtrace capture for 200 worst p999 traces per run (to examine reordering/KV edge cases)

Setup details (infra)
- Cluster: 8x A100 (40GB) dedicated pool, 16 concurrent slots per GPU, model: rw-m-7b-qlora (fairly typical long-sequence candidate), seq_len distribution: mix of short (avg 64) and medium (avg 512) with 5% long (2048)
- Traffic generator: locally instrumented harness that replays production sampling with controlled burst scaling; synthetic client supports configurable arrival jitter and bypass
- Profiling: CPU microtraces (sched wakeups), GPU kernel timestamps, KV cache hit/miss logs, per-request timeline (enqueue, admitted, dispatched, first-kv, response-start, response-end)

Commands / configs used (copied from test harness)
- scheduler config snippet used in tests:
  scheduling:
    cap_soft: ${cap_s}
    base_timeout_ms: ${base_timeout_ms}
    age_threshold_ms: ${age_threshold_ms}
    annealing_alpha: ${annealing_alpha}
    fairness_mode: ${fairness_mode}

Selected observations (concrete)
1) cap_s = 16, base_timeout_ms = 6, age_threshold = 50, anneal=0.75, fairness=age-priority (best baseline)
   - p999 reduced by ~28% compared to no-cap baseline (from 1.8s -> 1.3s)
   - p95 improved slightly (~6%)
   - p50 unchanged +/- 2%
   - GPU utilization reduced by 3% (we lost tiny amounts of packing efficiency)
   - Fraction of requests delayed >50ms increased from 1.2% -> 2.8% (age-priority kept worst-case bounded)
   - Microtraces show fewer long KV cache cold chains: large batches causing cache thrash were less frequent.

2) cap_s = 8 (aggressive), base_timeout=12
   - p99 improved but p90 regressed: often microbatched short requests waited longer to reach the cap, hurting median/90.
   - For latency-sensitive routes, this is unacceptable.

3) No cap, anneal only (alpha=0.5)
   - Small improvements at p99 but unstable under spikey traffic; anneal helps when arrivals are steady but overreacts when a burst fills many slots quickly.

4) fairness token-fairshare
   - Delivered best fairness (lowest starvation incidents) but slightly worse p999 than age-priority because tokens created a rigid admission cadence that allowed occasional large-batch backlogs.

Microtrace anecdotes
- Trace A (worst p999): long gap between 'dispatch' and 'first-kv' due to a prior gigantic batch that reclaimed GPU slot shortly after being scheduled. Uniformization runs replaced that huge batch with two mid-sized batches, and the long gap disappears.
- Trace B: when age_threshold was too low (20ms) we kept preempting batches and observed oscillation: requests ping-ponged between slots and saw increased tail due to repeated short waits. Age threshold tuning matters.

Hypotheses for why uniformization helps
- Reduces variance in GPU kernel queueing and KV cache churn. Many small/very large batches create context switches and cache pressure patterns that inflate long tails.
- Introducing controlled delays (soft cap + anneal) trades a bit of P50 for a large reduction in P999 because a modest wait avoids pathological packing.

Risks and downsides noted
- For ultra-low latency routes, any added waiting is bad: need route-level override to disable uniformization.
- Increased complexity: additional metrics to monitor and alert on (delays>age_threshold, oscillation patterns)
- Cost: slight utilization loss at times; should be acceptable if p999 SLAs are priority.

Practical recommendations (next step to stage for canary)
1) Ship feature gated behind route config: default off for latency-sensitive routes; opt-in beta for mid-tier.
2) Default params for canary: cap_soft=16, base_timeout_ms=6, age_threshold_ms=50, annealing_alpha=0.75, fairness=age-priority
3) Implement lightweight telemetry: per-route batch_size_entropy, fraction_delayed_over_age_threshold, p999_delta vs baseline, microtrace-sample-rate for worst 100 traces/day
4) Canary on dedicated pool with mixed traffic for 48h and compare tail regressions vs baseline with labels in rollout chart.

Open questions / TODOs
- What's the right cost tradeoff: quantify $/p999 improvement by running e2e cost simulations (tokens/sec * GPUhour) across a month of sampled traffic. (JIRA INF-2145)
- Could we use an ML model to predict imminent burst and preemptively adjust cap_soft rather than fixed heuristic? Quick prototype idea: short-window arrival-rate predictor -> cap adjustment.
- How does uniformization interact with KV cache prefetch heuristics? We should instrument KV cache warmup latency and explore prefetching keys for requests queued to become part of a forced split batch.
- Need A/B test design: can we run shadow traffic with uniformization on half of requests to measure user-facing quality regressions (generation quality / coherence) for text-heavy routes?

Notes to self / rough checklist
- [ ] Implement per-route feature flag and config override in router
- [ ] Add metrics to Grafana dashboard and alert rules on batch_entropy spike
- [ ] Create canary runplaybook + rollback criteria (p999 delta > 10% or p95 delta > 30%)
- [ ] PR: add unit tests for annealing math and age-bias ordering (see PR #487)

References and links
- JIRA INF-2145: proposal + cost-sim task
- GH PR #487: initial uniformization scheduler prototype
- Confluence: batch-uniformization design doc (internal)

Final thought (human)
This is promising as an operational lever: small controlled waits that reduce variance look more powerful for tail control than blunt caps or increasing capacity. The trick is not to over-tune and to guard latency-sensitive routes. Will discuss in Friday sync and try the canary next week.

Unresolved: tune age_threshold per-route automatically? We should be careful not to overfit to synthetic traces.
